context: §7.1 external-baseline campaign (edbd0b84) for prolix paper, sprint s71. Ran N=64 and N=512 benchmarks against DMFF, TorchMD, and espaloma before validating scope equivalence. Oracle consulted 2026-05-26.
lesson: Benchmark comparators must be category-equivalent before running any campaign. We produced 10,000× and 2800× headlines that are diagnostic of scope mismatch, not results. Three failure modes: (1) espaloma is a parameterization tool, not an MD engine — comparing prolix training step to espaloma MD step is a category error; (2) DMFF and TorchMD run full classical FF (bonded + LJ + Coulomb) while prolix Scope A is bonded-only; (3) DMFF CPU faster than DMFF GPU at N=512 because there is no batching and GPU launch overhead dominates — a single row like this causes reviewers to discount the entire table. The OpenMM parity harness (P2a in the roadmap) is the gate that should have been opened first: it forces a definitional audit of what each tool computes per step. The defensible story in the data is the scaling figure: prolix per-mol cost drops 5.3× from N=64→N=512 on A100; competitors are flat. That claim does not require scope equivalence on the per-step computation because it measures scaling slope, not intercept. Right comparators for the scaling figure are JAX-MD and kUPS (JAX-native, no N-batching), not DMFF/TorchMD/espaloma.
action: Before running any external-comparator benchmark campaign: (1) write the figure caption first — if it requires scope hedges larger than the figure itself, the design is wrong; (2) confirm all tools compute the same functional form per molecule-step; (3) confirm batching support is consistent across tools; (4) confirm tool category (MD engine vs parameterization tool vs differentiable optimizer). Open P2a (OpenMM parity harness) before running external benchmarks in future — it validates what prolix actually computes and makes scope-equivalence auditable.

context: §7.1 external-baseline campaign, sprint s71. The scaling signal (N=64→N=512 per-mol cost drop) was buried inside an invalid apples-to-oranges comparison table.
lesson: The real signal in a benchmarking campaign can be obscured by an invalid framing. Prolix drops 5.3× per-mol from N=64→N=512 on A100 while all competitors are flat — this is the heterogeneous-batching thesis in a single curve. But this was not the stated comparison; the stated comparison was raw speed vs DMFF/TorchMD/espaloma on what was assumed to be the same task. The scaling figure survives scope mismatch because it measures slope, not intercept. When a benchmark campaign produces headlines that seem implausibly large (10,000×), stop and ask whether the speedup measures the same computation, not whether the measurement is correct.
action: After any benchmark run, before extending to more hardware or larger N: verify the headline numbers are physically plausible given the computational difference between tools. A 10,000× speedup between two JAX programs doing bonded energy evaluation is a red flag, not a result. The figure caption test (can you write a non-hedged caption?) is the fastest gate.

context: Benchmarking prolix vs espaloma on pi_so3 (RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell, node4007). Campaign hp4-s71-external-baseline, SLURM job 15294138.
lesson: JAX workloads on Blackwell (SM120, node4007/node4008) require XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false. XLA autotuning hangs on SM120 even with jaxlib >= 0.4.38. Without it, a benchmark that takes 0.82 µs/mol-step appears to take 956 µs — a 1170x false slowdown that looks like an architectural disadvantage. Key the workaround on hostname/nodelist (node4007, node4008), not partition name: pi_so3 may gain non-Blackwell nodes over time.
action:
Add this block to every SLURM script that may land on node4007 or node4008:

```bash
_NODE="${SLURM_JOB_NODELIST:-$(hostname -s)}"
if [[ "${_NODE}" == *node4007* ]] || [[ "${_NODE}" == *node4008* ]]; then
    export XLA_FLAGS="${XLA_FLAGS:+${XLA_FLAGS} }--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false"
    echo "Blackwell workaround active (${_NODE}): XLA_FLAGS=${XLA_FLAGS}"
fi
```

The flag is a no-op on non-Blackwell hardware. When prolix results on Blackwell are 500x+ worse than H200, treat it as a toolchain artifact first — check XLA flags before investigating algorithm performance.

context: Adding DeprecationWarning for LangevinState re-export in prolix.batched_simulate. A fixer agent saw the __getattr__ branch and concluded the warning was already working, but the bare alias `LangevinState = _LangevinState` at line 36 was preventing it from ever firing.
lesson: A module-level `__getattr__(name)` (PEP 562) is ONLY invoked for names NOT found in the module `__dict__`. A bare assignment `Foo = _Foo` at module scope puts `Foo` into `__dict__`, making the __getattr__ branch for `'Foo'` permanently unreachable. When wiring a DeprecationWarning via __getattr__, always remove the bare alias — the two cannot coexist. Verify by asserting `'Name' not in module.__dict__` after the fix.
action: add

context: Reviewing a Haiku-tier fixer's diagnostic script (scripts/experiments/profile_b1_pme_grid_sweep.py, part of the B1 Phase 4 profiling investigation, task 260715_b1_physics_parity) before running it on the cluster. The fixer's own report claimed '--dry-run succeeded' as evidence of correctness.
lesson: logging.Logger.info() has no end= parameter, unlike print() -- a fixer wrote `log.info(f"...", end="")` to chain a line incrementally across several calls, mimicking print()'s pattern. This raised TypeError in the summary section, which runs AFTER the expensive per-grid-size GPU benchmark loop completes and BEFORE the JSON result is written -- meaning the crash would have silently discarded all real benchmark data on the first real (non-dry-run) invocation. The fixer's own '--dry-run succeeded' claim was true but irrelevant: dry-run mode exits before ever reaching the buggy summary code, so it structurally could not have caught this.
action: Never trust a fixer's self-reported dry-run/smoke-test success as proof a script is correct end-to-end -- read the actual diff and trace which code paths the smoke test does and does not exercise. When reviewing any log.info()/log.warning() call built from an f-string with unusual kwargs, check the call against logging.Logger's real signature -- print()-style kwargs (end, sep, flush) are a common, easy mistake that only crashes at the tail end of an otherwise-successful run.

context: Building a Phase 4 profiling script (scripts/experiments/profile_b1_water_trace.py, task 260715_b1_physics_parity) to inspect B1's compiled water-class HLO. Found zero PME/FFT instructions anywhere in the compiled program and chased it down with 4 independent tests rather than assuming the script itself was wrong.
lesson: physics_system_from_bundle (src/prolix/api/bundle_md.py) converts MolecularBundle's DYNAMIC fields (deliberately kept traceable, by design, to avoid recompiling per topology) into PhysicsSystem fields declared eqx.field(static=True) -- static because real FFT grid dimensions genuinely need compile-time constants. pme_alpha and nonbonded_cutoff already had a safe fallback for this conversion (_host_float: try float(x), except ConcretizationTypeError: return a scoped default) because under EnsemblePlan's real stacked/vmapped dispatch the bundle field is a genuine BatchTracer, not a concrete value, even when every replica in the stack is physically identical (vmap doesn't know that a priori). box_size was NOT given the same treatment -- it was derived unconditionally (jnp.diag(bundle.box)), so a live tracer landed in a static field. Assigning a tracer to an eqx.field(static=True) does not error at construction time (Equinox just warns 'A JAX array is being set as static!'); it fails LATER, silently, wherever downstream code tries to concretize a value derived from it (int()/float() calls) -- and that failure was caught by a deliberately broad `except (TypeError, ValueError, ConcretizationTypeError)` meant only for a legitimate one-time jax.eval_shape probe, so it silently disabled the entire PME reciprocal-space contribution instead of raising. This had been running unnoticed since the fix that introduced the pattern for pme_alpha/nonbonded_cutoff didn't get applied consistently to every field bridging the same dynamic-to-static boundary.
action: When a bridge function converts ANY dynamic/traceable field into a field declared eqx.field(static=True) (or any other framework's 'must be concrete/hashable' marker), audit EVERY field making that crossing, not just the one that happened to break first -- the fix for one field (pme_alpha's _host_float fallback) does not imply the pattern was applied uniformly. Treat 'A JAX array is being set as static!' warnings as a real signal to investigate, not background noise -- it fired on every relevant test throughout this whole investigation and was the earliest available clue. When a broad except clause is justified by one specific caller's need (here, jax.eval_shape's abstract probe), verify empirically that it isn't ALSO silently catching a different, illegitimate failure from a different caller -- a silently-empty/no-op result under an exception handler is invisible unless you specifically test with the feature toggled (e.g. compare real trajectories under two different parameter values that should diverge).

context: After fixing the box_size static-field bug, PME reciprocal energy still showed zero FFT ops in the compiled HLO for B1's water class. Bypassed the broad except clause to capture the real exception rather than assuming the first fix was sufficient.
lesson: A second, independent bug was masked by the same broad except clause: _pme_reciprocal_and_corrections' exclusion-correction branch (taken whenever implicit_solvent=False, which is how B1's water class always calls it) derived 1-2/1-3/1-4 excluded atom pairs via topology.find_bonded_exclusions -- a function that does pure Python/numpy graph traversal (collections.defaultdict adjacency list, nested Python for-loops, np.array(bonds)) on the bond topology. This kind of host-only computation cannot run under jax.vmap/jax.jit tracing AT ALL, regardless of any fallback-default pattern -- it raised TracerArrayConversionError (a TypeError subclass, so it was also silently caught by the same except (TypeError, ...) clause meant for the box_size probe). Unlike the box_size bug (fixable with a scoped-default fallback, since the value only needs to be 'close enough' when untraceable), there is no safe fallback for exclusion pairs -- the correction is physically large (a raw uncorrected reciprocal energy of -260 kcal/mol vs a correct, exclusion-corrected -0.15 kcal/mol at this system's scale) and system-specific, so it must be precomputed. Fixed by reusing bundle.excl_indices/excl_scales_elec -- already precomputed host-side at bundle-CONSTRUCTION time (always concrete, before any jax.jit/vmap boundary) for the dense direct-space nonbonded path -- via a new per-pair vmap-safe correction function, instead of recomputing 1-2/1-3/1-4 groups from raw bonds a second time inside the traced region.
action: Two DIFFERENT bug classes can hide behind one broad except clause, and fixing the first one you find is not evidence the symptom is resolved -- re-run the SAME empirical test (not just re-read the code) after every fix to confirm the exception is actually gone, not just changed. When any function does host-only work (Python control flow over array VALUES, not just shapes -- graph traversal, dict/set building, per-element branching) on data that could plausibly be traced under vmap/jit elsewhere in the codebase, that computation must be precomputed at construction time and carried as data, not recomputed lazily inside the traced call -- there is no exception-handling fallback that can rescue a fundamentally non-traceable algorithm, only a scoped-default fallback for a SINGLE VALUE with a known-reasonable substitute. Before reusing an existing precomputed field for a new purpose (bundle.excl_indices was built for the dense LJ/Coulomb path), verify the scale-factor SEMANTICS actually match what the new caller needs (here: 'fraction of interaction to keep' meant the same thing in both the dense direct-space scaling and the PME reciprocal-space correction, which was not obvious a priori and needed checking against the correction formula, not assumed).

context: Submitting B1 Phase 4 profiling runs to engaging via myxcel_submit_job, each wrapped in `bth run --campaign 32d6574e -- ...`. The campaign was created locally (`bth campaign create`) before submission, matching documented sequencing.
lesson: Two separate remote-execution gaps discovered in the same submission, both worth remembering together since they're easy to conflate: (1) mcp__myxcel__push_project silently pushed the WRONG source tree -- it resolves the registered project root (the main non-worktree checkout at ~/projects/prolix, still on an old branch/commit), not the calling session's actual git worktree (.claude/worktrees/<name>/), even though the session is running from and committing to the worktree. The push reported success with no error, and only direct SSH inspection (grep for a known-new symbol in the remote file) revealed the code was stale -- the SLURM job then failed with a plain 'file not found' for a script that definitely existed locally. Fixed by rsyncing directly from the worktree to the remote path instead of using the project-root-based push. (2) Independently, bathos campaigns are local-catalog entities -- creating one locally does not make it resolvable by a REMOTE bathos instance's `bth run --campaign <id>` call, since local and remote catalogs are separate until explicitly `bth sync`'d, and campaigns are not part of what gets pushed by a code-sync step. The remote run recorded the literal unresolved campaign_id string and its sidecar outcome gate evaluated to 'unknown' rather than pass/marginal/fail. Fixed after the fact via `bth campaign add <run_id> --campaign <full-uuid>` once the full UUID was found via `bth sql`, but the automatic outcome-gate evaluation did not retroactively re-fire.
action: Before trusting ANY 'push succeeded' report for a worktree-based session, verify by grepping the remote file directly for a known-new symbol/string introduced in the very latest local commit -- do not trust the push tool's own success/byte-count summary, which can report success while silently syncing from the wrong source directory entirely. When submitting bathos-tracked cluster jobs, treat the campaign as needing its own explicit sync/linkage step separate from code sync -- either sync the catalog to the remote BEFORE submitting (if that's supported) or budget for a post-hoc `bth campaign add` pass per run after pulling results back, and don't expect the outcome gate to have evaluated correctly for such runs without checking `bth campaign review` for an 'unknown' anomaly count.

context: Building solvate_protein_to_bundle (task 260715_b1_physics_parity, src/prolix/physics/solvation.py) to test heterogeneous batching of real solvated proteins. Verified the new adapter's energy against pad_solvated_system/single_padded_energy_nl_cvjp (the pathway test_solvated_explicit_integration.py already uses) rather than trusting a plausible-looking finite number.
lesson: _pme_reciprocal_and_corrections (src/prolix/batched_energy.py) called explicit_corrections.lj_dispersion_tail_energy(box, sigma, epsilon, cutoff, n_tail) where n_tail was a SCALAR real-atom count (sys.n_real_atoms), but the function's 5th parameter is named atom_mask and expects an (N,)-shaped array -- it does `atom_mask.astype(jnp.float32)` then elementwise-multiplies every atom's sigma^3/sigma^6 term by it. Passing a scalar broadcasts that scalar across every real atom's term (instead of masking each atom 0/1), inflating the C6/C12 sums by a factor of n_atoms; since the final energy formula SQUARES those sums, the resulting error scales as n_atoms^2. For B1's water class (12 real atoms) this was a ~144x inflation of an already-tiny correction term, invisible against the ~kcal/mol-scale PME terms that dominate a 4-water system's total energy. For a 1963-atom solvated protein (the first system to actually stress-test this branch at real-protein scale) it produced a -130-million-kcal/mol energy from what should have been a small long-range dispersion correction -- an error four orders of magnitude larger than the whole rest of the system's energy combined, on a system where the standalone bonded terms (bond/angle/dihedral, ~85/22/237 kcal/mol) all looked completely normal.
action: When a function parameter is literally NAMED after what it expects (atom_mask, not n_atoms or count), passing anything else through it -- even a value that happens to be numerically related (a count derived from summing the very mask that should have been passed) -- will not raise a shape error if the function's internal math tolerates scalar broadcasting, so it can silently corrupt results by orders of magnitude with no exception anywhere. When a bug's damage scales with a hidden power of system size (here, n^2 from a sum-then-square pattern), a small test system can make the bug numerically invisible even when it is 100% present and 100% wrong -- this is exactly why the same _pme_reciprocal_and_corrections function passed every water-class (n=12) test in this codebase for months while this bug sat right next to two other real bugs (box_size static-field leak, host-only find_bonded_exclusions under tracing) already found and fixed in the same function earlier today. Before trusting any energy/physics function at a NEW, larger scale than it has previously been exercised at, sanity-check each additive energy component individually (not just the final total) -- a single absurd component is easy to spot in isolation and easy to miss when summed into a total that merely looks 'large but maybe plausible for a big system.'

context: Testing solvate_protein_to_bundle (commit 89ef602) under EnsemblePlan's real stacked dispatch with genuinely heterogeneous (2 different real proteins) bundles -- the first time this morning's box_size fix (commit 395995b) was exercised with real variation across replicas rather than replicated copies of one template.
lesson: _host_box_size's fallback default (added in commit 395995b) was a MODULE-LEVEL jnp.array(...) constant (_DEFAULT_PBC_BOX_SIZE), referenced as a shared Python object across every call, including calls made from inside many different jax.jit trace contexts (repeated EnsemblePlan.run() invocations, each building a fresh @jax.jit closure per ensemble_plan.py:420). This raised 'UnexpectedTracerError: leaked intermediate value' -- a function transformed by JAX had a side effect, allowing a reference to an intermediate value to escape the transformation's scope. B1's water-class tests never hit this because the fallback path there is exercised far less variably (one topology tiled to itself, not genuinely different systems across replicas). It reproduced reliably the first time two DIFFERENT real proteins were dispatched together.
action: Never define a JAX array (jnp.array(...)) as a module-level constant that gets referenced as a default/fallback value INSIDE a function that will be called from many different jax.jit trace contexts over a process's lifetime -- construct it fresh (from a plain Python tuple/list held at module level, converted to jnp.array at call time) inside the function instead. This is a general JAX gotcha, not specific to this bug: shared JAX array objects crossing trace-context boundaries can carry stale tracer associations forward even when the array itself looks like an ordinary concrete value. The fix pattern is simple and cheap (store the plain Python tuple at module scope, wrap in jnp.array() at the point of use) -- worth applying by default to ANY fallback-default JAX array in this codebase, not just retrofitting after a crash, since single-topology-only testing (like B1's water class) can leave this class of bug latent for a long time before something exercises the fallback path with enough real trace-context diversity to surface it.

context: P4 (Stage 1 CPU micro-probe with trace capture) of the jax-profiling-optimization-workflow spec required resolving, before writing scripts/profiling/trace.py, exactly HOW a named_scope label surfaces in a jax.profiler.trace Perfetto capture -- the spec named three candidate forms (nested duration slice, /-delimited op-name prefix, TraceAnnotation/XLA-Modules row) and required recording the answer in step notes before coding the parser.
lesson: Do NOT assume a jax.named_scope label appears anywhere in the executed trace.json.gz itself on CPU (XLA CPU backend) -- it does not, in any of the three forms the spec anticipated, on the trace events themselves. Concretely: (1) the executed trace's per-thunk 'X'-phase events are named after the POST-FUSION HLO thunk/op name (e.g. 'wrapped_multiply', 'reduce_add_fusion'), carried in args['hlo_op']/args['hlo_module'] -- these names carry zero named_scope information. (2) The named_scope path DOES survive, but only in the separately-obtained COMPILED HLO text (jax.jit(fn).lower(*args).compile().as_text()), as a '/'-delimited prefix on each instruction's metadata={op_name="jit(fn)/scope1/scope2/.../leaf_op"} field. (3) Therefore per-scope wall-clock attribution needs a TWO-INPUT pipeline: parse the executed trace for exclusive durations/counts keyed by hlo_op thunk name, AND separately parse the compiled HLO text to build a thunk-name -> scope-path mapping (resolving via calls=/to_apply= references down through nested computations when the top-level ENTRY instruction itself carries no metadata -- its callee's ROOT instruction usually does). Attribute each instruction's own scope by taking the DEEPEST known label in its resolved path (search backwards through path segments after stripping a leading jit(...) prefix and excluding the final leaf-primitive-name segment). (4) A useful, non-obvious byproduct of the same investigation: DISPATCH_COUNT's 4th originally-planned counter, n_host_syncs (device->host transfer count), is NOT derivable on CPU either -- repeated block_until_ready() calls on an already-computed array produce ZERO additional trace signal (CPU device buffers ARE host memory, so there is structurally nothing to transfer/count). n_executions (ExecuteReplicated.__call__ events), n_compilations (official jax.monitoring event /jax/core/compile/backend_compile_duration, or the Perfetto 'backend_compile_and_load' event name), and n_jit_traces (official jax.monitoring event /jax/core/compile/jaxpr_trace_duration, or Perfetto 'PjitFunction(<fn_name>)' events) ARE all cleanly derivable and were kept in the contract.
action: When implementing or documenting jax.profiler.trace-based named_scope attribution (P7's GPU probe, or the P9 xtrax jax-profiling skill), always cross-reference the compiled HLO text's op_name metadata against the executed trace's hlo_op thunk names via a resolve-through-calls/to_apply chain -- do not assume the executed trace alone carries scope information, and do not assume the GPU trace shape matches this CPU finding without re-running the same dump-and-inspect investigation P4 did.

context: P5's A/B perturbation gate (scripts/explore/prof_stage1_scope_perturbation.py) times a target function with named_scope wraps on vs off, to check whether the wraps change XLA fusion decisions. The functions were initially timed by calling eqx.filter_grad(fn)/jax.grad(fn) directly, with '3 untimed warm-up calls' meant to absorb JIT compile per the spec.
lesson: eqx.filter_grad/jax.grad alone do NOT compile a function -- without an explicit outer jax.jit, every call (including the 'warm-up' ones) runs in eager per-op dispatch mode. Confirmed directly: median call time was ~0.86s on a trivial N=64 system (vs ~1-3ms once jitted), ~280x slower, and the warm-up step absorbed nothing because there was no compile to absorb. This isn't just a performance bug -- it's a correctness bug for this specific measurement's whole premise: XLA fusion is fundamentally a compile-time decision, so an eager (un-jitted) measurement has NO fusion to perturb and would silently report a meaningless PASS on every run regardless of what the code under test actually does.
action: Whenever building a timing harness meant to detect a fusion-level effect (operator fusion, scope-boundary perturbation, kernel-selection changes), always wrap the measured function in jax.jit explicitly and verify the warm-up calls are actually paying a real compile cost (e.g. by checking the warm-up is dramatically slower than the timed reps, or checking n_compilations via jax.profiler.trace) before trusting any comparison built on top of it.

context: P5's scopes_off arm patches jax.named_scope to a no-op before importing prolix, matching the spec's 'contextlib.nullcontext-equivalent' instruction. The first implementation used `jax.named_scope = lambda *a, **k: contextlib.nullcontext()`.
lesson: This crashed immediately with `TypeError: 'nullcontext' object is not callable` the moment any prolix import pulled in equinox, because equinox's own eqx.nn module decorates methods with `@named_scope("...")` at class-definition (import) time -- i.e. jax.named_scope's real object supports BOTH `with named_scope(x):` (context manager) AND `@named_scope(x)` (decorator) usage. contextlib.nullcontext instances implement __enter__/__exit__ but are not callable, so they satisfy the first usage and break the second. Any monkeypatch of a dual-purpose (context-manager + decorator) API needs to preserve both call shapes, not just the more commonly-seen one.
action: When monkeypatching jax.named_scope (or any similarly dual-purpose JAX/library API) to a no-op, use a small class extending contextlib.ContextDecorator (with __enter__ returning self and __exit__ returning False) instead of contextlib.nullcontext, so the replacement is usable both as `with x():` and `@x()`.

context: P5's perturbation gate runs two independent statistical checks (whole_step, tile_function), each spawning many paired subprocesses that write pair{i}_on.json/pair{i}_off.json/.forces.npy files keyed only by a process-local integer counter starting at 0, into one shared out_dir passed on the command line.
lesson: Launching both checks as separate concurrent background processes against the SAME out_dir caused them to write to IDENTICAL paths (pair0_on.json, pair1_on.json, ...) simultaneously, since pair indices reset to 0 for each independent run rather than being globally unique. One run finished and printed a plausible-looking, self-consistent summary (real-looking statistics, sensible verdict) that was nonetheless untrustworthy, because there was no way to rule out a write-order collision during the overlap window. Plausible output is not evidence of correctness when a known race condition could have produced it -- this needed to be treated as corrupted and discarded, not spot-checked and accepted.
action: Any harness that (a) spawns multiple independent runs/configurations concurrently and (b) writes per-iteration artifacts keyed by a small process-local counter must give each run/configuration its own output subdirectory (or otherwise globally-unique naming), not just a shared parent directory -- do this from the start, not after observing a suspicious result, since a race can produce output that looks completely fine.

context: Launching P5's long-running gate script as a background task, first via `nohup uv run ... > $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/log 2>&1 & disown` inside a Bash tool call with run_in_background:true set on that same call.
lesson: Two distinct, compounding environment traps: (1) nesting shell-level backgrounding (&, with or without nohup/disown) inside a tool-level run_in_background:true call means the OUTER tracked command (which backgrounds instantly and returns) is reported 'completed' by the harness within ~1 second, and the sandboxed session backing that specific tool invocation is torn down at that point -- silently killing the detached child process too, despite nohup/disown (which only block SIGHUP, not whatever teardown actually happens). This happened twice, with zero error signal -- no log file, no output, process simply gone. (2) Separately, $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp -- freely writable in every FOREGROUND Bash call all session -- is READ-ONLY specifically under run_in_background:true (confirmed via a minimal `echo hello > $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/test.log` background command failing with 'Read-only file system'). A background command's own stdout/stderr redirection can fail with no visible symptom other than a missing log file.
action: For a genuinely long-running background command: (a) never nest your own shell-level backgrounding (&, nohup, disown) inside a run_in_background:true tool call -- run the real long-lived command as the SOLE foreground command of that call, and let the tool's own tracking keep it alive; (b) redirect any log output to a worktree-relative path (e.g. under outputs/, gitignored) rather than $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp, since the latter is not reliably writable under background execution even though it is under foreground execution; (c) after launching, confirm the task is genuinely progressing (e.g. via growing output files or ps aux) before trusting a 'running' status, since a silently-killed process and a genuinely-running one can look identical in early monitoring.

context: Planning Prolix full-step MD defaults after a force-only vs full-MD profiling campaign. Three nonbonded paths exist: dense all-pairs autodiff, Flash tiled all-pairs (same pair set, memory algorithm + remat), and neighbor-list O(N·K) cutoff. An early plan draft said: if NL loses to Flash on DHFR, default Flash and file NL as a remaining kernel gap. That was caught in review as the same jumping-to-conclusions failure mode seen on multiple projects.
lesson: When the algorithmically cheaper intended path loses a benchmark to a more expensive fallback, treat that as a defect investigation, not as permission to ship the fallback. Do not collapse 'which pairs / which algorithm' with 'which memory strategy for the same pairs.' Do not write production defaults as consolation prizes for an unexplained race. Flash (or any tiled all-pairs kernel) is a valid default only for all-pairs physics, or after the cutoff path is shown to be a correct O(N·K) implementation and still loses for a documented reason (e.g. K≈N). Never promote a naive dense path just because it is the implicit flag combination.
action: Before flipping defaults or declaring a kernel gap from a timing table: (1) name the pair set and complexity class of each cell (all-pairs vs cutoff vs dense tape); (2) confirm init and step use the same backend (no silent dense first-force); (3) inspect rebuild cadence, padding/K, exclusion convention, and whether neighbor= actually reaches the energy; (4) only then decide defaults. If the intended path still loses, document the residual reason — do not default the winner by framing.

context: Implementing #4383 (1vii NL nonbonded-energy parity vs vendored OpenMM gold) surfaced a real AC2/AC3 failure (energy off by -5305 kcal/mol, force RMSE 71.4 kcal/mol/A with a 3168 kcal/mol/A single-atom outlier). Root-caused via finite-difference-vs-jax.grad comparison on the actual energy_fn: finite-diff of prolix's own energy function matched OpenMM gold forces almost exactly (e.g. atom 6092: fd=[-2032.14, 2310.29, -764.16] vs gold=[-2032.13, 2310.35, -764.23]), while jax.grad on the identical function returned near-zero, disconnected values ([3.76, 1.46, -13.84] for the same atom) -- proving the physics/exclusion implementation was correct and jax.grad itself was broken for this code path.
lesson: chunked_lj_energy_nl and chunked_coulomb_energy_nl (src/prolix/physics/optimization.py) both define a custom_vjp (defvjp) whose backward pass unconditionally zeros the gradient not just for the two genuinely non-differentiable integer arguments (excl_indices, neighbor_idx -- correct) but ALSO for r (positions), charges, and excl_scales (all real-valued, genuinely differentiable -- wrong). This looks like an incomplete stub: the dense-branch sibling (chunked_coulomb_energy, no _nl suffix, same file) has a correct analytical backward pass (f_tile_grad/pair_vals computing real dE/dd), but the NL/tiled-neighbor-list variants never got the equivalent treatment. It went undetected because the only prior test exercising these NL kernels via jax.grad -- the two-particle water/flash probe (nonbonded_omm_parity/lj_oracle.py's compare_nl_two_particle) -- uses a geometry deliberately placed inside the LJ switch window where the TRUE force happens to be small, so 'gradient is always exactly zero' produced a coincidentally tiny RMSE (0.002) that looked like a pass. Production dynamics code sidesteps this entirely by using FlashMD's analytical forces (force_fn_from_bundle / single_padded_force) rather than jax.grad through the NL branch, so this bug had no other surface to manifest on until a real-scale system with genuinely large forces (#4383's solvated 1VII, 7507 atoms) was differentiated through energy_fn_from_bundle's NL path for the first time.
action: Before trusting any jax.grad/custom_vjp result on a new code path (especially one gated behind a defvjp), do a finite-difference sanity check against the SAME energy function on a real (not toy/coincidental-geometry) system BEFORE comparing against an external oracle -- this isolates 'is my own autodiff correct' from 'does my physics match ground truth' and would have caught this bug in minutes instead of requiring cluster-based debugging after an external-parity failure. When a custom_vjp backward pass returns jnp.zeros_like(x) for an argument, that argument's docstring/comment must explicitly justify WHY (e.g. 'x is a non-differentiable integer index') -- a blanket zero-gradient template copy-pasted across multiple real-valued and integer-valued arguments in the same return tuple is a red flag worth auditing on sight. A toy/2-particle regression test that passes with near-zero true force provides much weaker gradient-correctness coverage than it appears to -- prefer at least one real-scale, genuinely-large-force regression case for any kernel whose gradient correctness matters.

context: While reconciling #4793 (flash-vs-dense speedup contradiction) and fixing #4623 (NL custom_vjp), only measured 1VII (~2000 atoms) initially -- concluded dense was the clear winner and flash/NL were both worse. context: prolix task 260903_dhfr_nl_capacity (2026-09-03). A DHFR neighbor-list run died with 'Neighbor list overflowed ... capacity formula (compute_nl_capacity) likely needs a larger safety_factor for this system.' The single-bundle path that raised it never calls compute_nl_capacity at all -- it was byte-identical to the stacked path up to the make_neighbor_list_fn call, then stopped at a bare neighbor_fn.allocate(). Raising safety_factor could not have moved it by a single slot.
lesson: A diagnostic must name the knob the FAILING path actually reads, not the knob that governs the same concept elsewhere in the codebase. This message pointed at a parameter with no causal connection to the failure, and would have done so for every future reader. The fix is cheap and compounding: report what was allocated, what the formula recommended, how many retries were attempted, and which code path is speaking. Once rewritten that way, every later failure in the same sprint was readable in one glance -- including the one that turned out to be an entirely different bug. Test for it: when two code paths implement the same concept by different rules, an error raised by one must never name the other's parameters. Better, give them one shared helper so the divergence cannot recur -- that is what actually fixed it here.
action: When writing or reviewing a resource/config error, check that every parameter it names is genuinely read by the path that raises it. If two paths compute the same quantity differently, unify them behind one helper rather than documenting the difference in prose.

context: prolix task 260903_dhfr_nl_capacity (2026-09-03). Diagnosing a DHFR trajectory that looked like it was collapsing, I wrote a per-chunk displacement metric as raw norm(positions - prev_positions). It reported ~2 A/step mean and 151 A max, implying ~1e7 K, and I was one message away from reporting that. But jax_md's space.periodic wraps coordinates into [0, box) every step, so a boundary crossing reads as a ~62 A jump for an atom that actually moved 0.2 A. Adding the minimum-image correction changed the numbers to 1.2-1.5 A/step and max pinned at sqrt(3)*L/2, the geometric ceiling.
lesson: The BATHOS 'verify your measurement pipeline before trusting a research conclusion' rule applies to the throwaway diagnostic you just wrote, not only to the project's tracked code. A diagnostic written in five minutes to investigate a bug is itself an instrument, and an unvalidated one -- it gets no review, no test, and its output is maximally persuasive precisely when it is most dramatic. Here the conclusion happened to survive (the system really is ~250x too fast), but the headline number was inflated ~1.6x by my own artifact, and it could just as easily have been the whole effect. The sanity check that catches this class costs seconds: the metric must be right for the SIMPLEST case, and for anything under periodic boundaries that means asking 'what does this report for an atom that merely crossed a boundary?' Note the companion tell: in the same script min_dist WAS minimum-image corrected while displacement was not, so the file contained both the correct idiom and the bug.
action: Before quoting a number from an ad-hoc diagnostic, state what it would report for a known-trivial input (an atom that moved zero but wrapped; an empty set; a single element). Under PBC specifically, every distance or displacement must be minimum-image corrected -- grep your own script for the raw subtraction.

context: prolix task 260903_dhfr_nl_capacity (2026-09-03). A neighbor-list buffer overflowed at DHFR scale. The obvious reading was 'the buffer is too small', and the error message said so. I fixed the sizing properly (both construction sites now share one rule) and it still overflowed, having grown 768 -> 5887. Needing >5887 neighbors in a 9.5 A sphere is ~15x liquid density -- physically impossible for a well-behaved system. The buffer was not undersized; the quantity it was sizing was unbounded, because the trajectory was diverging (~250x too-fast atoms, later filed as #4953). Chunked running never overflowed at all, because re-allocating every 20 steps let the buffer chase the divergence.
lesson: A resource-exhaustion error (buffer overflow, OOM, capacity exceeded, retry limit) is a claim about a RATE, not about a size. Before enlarging the resource, establish that the demand is bounded at all: compute what the physically or logically correct value should be and compare. Here the arithmetic took one line -- at the system's known density a cutoff sphere holds ~380 atoms, so any requirement above ~1000 was evidence of a different bug entirely, and no capacity value would ever have been enough. Enlarging the buffer would have converted a loud, correct failure into a silent wrong answer. The corollary matters just as much: the path that raises such an error is often the ONLY detector of a system-wide problem. Here the flash force path and OpenMM both ran the same diverging system without complaint because neither asserts anything; the neighbor-list path was the only component in either engine that noticed, and every throughput number the benchmark had ever published was a timing of a broken system. Ask what the failing check was detecting before you relax it.
action: On any capacity/OOM/retry-limit failure, first compute the value the resource SHOULD need from first principles and compare to what was requested. If the requested value is physically implausible, stop -- the bug is upstream. Never raise a limit to make a check pass without that comparison.

context: prolix task 260903_dhfr_nl_capacity (2026-09-03). Investigating why a DHFR trajectory was 'collapsing', I tested five specific structural mechanisms in sequence, each a separate ~4-minute cluster job: unconstrained water, ghost/padding-atom drift, SETTLE not engaging, wrong water parameters, dt/kT placeholder leakage. All five were falsified. Only then did I measure the primary observable -- how far atoms actually move per step -- which immediately showed ~250x the thermal expectation and reframed the whole problem from 'collapse' to 'explosion'. That single measurement would have ruled out most of the five mechanisms up front, since a thermostat holding a wildly wrong temperature is not a geometry problem.
lesson: Measure the phenomenon before testing mechanisms for it. Each of the five hypotheses was individually cheap and plausible, so the sequence felt like progress -- but they were all answers to 'which component is broken?' when I had not yet established WHAT was broken in quantitative terms. The project's own BATHOS heuristic states the trigger explicitly: falsify three hypotheses in a row and stop, because the probability that every hypothesis was wrong drops sharply and the measurement is probably the thing to interrogate. I read that rule, cited it after the second falsification, and then kept hypothesis-testing anyway. Characterise first: what is the magnitude, does it grow or saturate, is it the same across the paths you can vary. Those answers partition the hypothesis space instead of sampling it one point at a time. Naming the phenomenon wrongly compounds it -- calling this a 'collapse' primed five geometry hypotheses, when the data said the atoms were simply moving far too fast.
action: Before testing any specific mechanism, measure the primary observable and its magnitude, growth, and invariance across the dimensions you can cheaply vary. If you falsify two hypotheses in a row, stop generating a third and go measure instead.

context: 260903_dhfr_divergence_parity, 2026-09-04, prolix #4953/#4971. I briefly read that as 'the fix did not help' and started reaching for another mechanism. A changed numerical path on a GPU almost always perturbs the last digits; exact float equality across a rerun means the branch was never entered. Check the enclosing guard before doubting the physics. Corollary: a feature gated on an optional argument that defaults to None is silently disabled for every caller that forgets it -- grep the call sites before trusting that the guard is ever true.

context: 260903_dhfr_divergence_parity, 2026-09-04, prolix #4972. A regression gate came back 1 failed / 48 passed right after I changed core physics. The obvious readings were 'I broke it' or 'it was already broken'; I had evidence for neither, because the file carried module-level pytest.mark.slow and CI runs -m 'not (slow or ...)', so it had not run anywhere in a long time. Instead of picking, I wrote a slurm job that runs the SAME test twice on the SAME node with the same seed, differing only in whether my change is present -- stripping it by sed on its own marker comment and restoring via an EXIT/INT/TERM trap. Both legs failed identically (23.11s vs 23.22s): pre-existing. Later a second gate timed out; same discipline showed it ran on node2403 while the passing one ran on node4007, a ~5x slower box, and the timing-out test did not even use the changed code path.
lesson: When a test fails right after your change, assuming it is a pre-existing failure is exactly as unfounded as assuming it is your regression. Measure it: run the same test with and without the change, same node, same seed, one variable. It costs one job and converts an argument into a fact. Two corollaries: (1) before comparing runs, check they were on the same hardware -- a cluster job that lands on a different node is not a controlled comparison, and a timeout is usually about the node, not the code; (2) a test excluded from CI by a marker has no known state, so its failure carries no information about when it broke until you establish a baseline.

context: 260903_dhfr_divergence_parity, 2026-09-04, prolix #4972. A physics test asserted mean temperature < 350 K and reported 484.43 K, its own message guessing 'Gate 2 may be incomplete'. The tempting fix was to relax the threshold to match. Instead I read its parameters: n_waters=2, dt=2.0 fs, gamma=1.0 ps^-1 -- 4x the documented timestep cap, in the small-N regime, with weak friction, which are the three conditions the project's own CLAUDE.md each says require dt <= 0.5 fs. So the assertion may simply have been unachievable in any supported configuration. I swept both variables using the test's OWN helper (importing the test module rather than reimplementing, so the measurement could not differ). Result: at n=2 the bar is only cleared at dt=0.25 fs, but at n=64 it lands on 299.65 K at the same 2.0 fs. Size was the variable. The numbers also reproduced an earlier campaign's documented size crossover to within a degree.
lesson: Before changing a failing assertion, read the test's PARAMETERS against the envelope the project documents as supported. A test can be wrong not in its threshold but in the configuration it measures -- asserting a property in a regime where the docs already say it does not hold. Fix it by moving the measurement into the supported regime (one variable), not by loosening the bar to fit the observed number; the latter converts a broken test into a broken guarantee. Sweep with the test's own helper, imported, so a reimplementation cannot be what explains the discrepancy. And when your sweep reproduces an independent prior campaign's numbers, that agreement is the evidence that licenses trusting the result.

context: 260903_dhfr_divergence_parity, 2026-09-04, prolix #4953. Six mechanisms had already been proposed and falsified for a trajectory divergence (unconstrained water, ghost-atom drift, SETTLE not engaging, wrong water parameters, a force sign error, missing exclusions). I killed a seventh of my own within the hour by parsing the fixture. Only then did I stop hypothesising and build instruments: a single-point per-term force comparison against OpenMM on the identical configuration, and a from-rest Newton invariant (thermostat off, one step must give exactly 0.5*(F/m)*dt^2). Forces came back within 0.039%; C/N/S landed on a ratio of exactly 1.000 while 1011 atoms -- precisely 3 x 337 whole water molecules, water fraction 1.0000 against a 0.894 baseline -- moved 8-9 A with normal forces. Both root causes fell out in one session after weeks of guessing.
lesson: The instruments that find a bug are usually cheaper than the hypotheses that miss it, and they should come FIRST once one or two guesses have failed. Two shapes did all the work here. (1) Compare against an independent implementation on the identical input, decomposed by term, and report cosine similarity beside RMSE -- a cosine near 1 with a magnitude ratio far from 1 is a units/prefactor bug, and RMSE alone hides both. (2) Test an invariant with a closed form against synthetic ground truth: from rest with the thermostat off, displacement must equal 0.5*(F/m)*dt^2, and any deviation is a pure number whose value names the defect (mass-valued -> momentum/velocity confusion; constant -> a dt or unit factor). Also: group the residual by a physical key (here atomic mass, and water-vs-protein). A single scalar ratio cannot distinguish '12x for carbon' from '12x for everything', and a median near 0.3 beside a mean near 200 is the tell that you have a tail, not a scale error.
action: add

context: Pallas v2.4 end-to-end multi-bucket / multi-replica MD optimization across ragged size buckets (6,658-atom ubiquitin and 4,200-atom systems in 8,192 / 25,000 buckets, 23,558-atom solvated DHFR + mutant in 25,000 bucket) on Blackwell sm_120, Ampere A100 sm_80, and Ada L4 sm_89.

context: Debugging and optimizing stacked multi-replica / heterogeneous-bucket EnsemblePlan.run(run_mode="inference", use_neighbor_list=True, use_pallas=True) at B >= 2 on solvated DHFR (61.645 A box) and heterogeneous same-bucket bundles.

Always extract host_box_vec on the host before @jax.jit / vmap and replace bundle.box with a concrete np.ndarray on the energy-construction bundle. (2) Shared NeighborList seed sizing for heterogeneous buckets: allocating the shared NL seed from bundles[0] overflows when bundles[1] is denser, while calling neighbor_fn.allocate per bundle produces mismatched cell_list_capacity PyTree leaves. Allocate once on the densest bundle using the union atom_mask across the bucket, pad columns in O(1), and update remaining bundles via seed_invalidated.update(b_pos). (3) Cache compiled stacked runs in _STACKED_INFERENCE_CACHE with n_steps passed as a dynamic int32 array into lax.while_loop, and ensure _run_single_inference trims output to bundle.n_atoms whenever trim_output=True regardless of integration_prefix.
action: Propagate concrete host_box_vec into _setup_integrator under vmap, allocate shared NL seeds once on densest_bundle with union_mask, and cache stacked inference runs in _STACKED_INFERENCE_CACHE with dynamic n_steps.

context: Pallas v2.5/v2.6 single-launch megakernel (MK-36..MK-40) and float32 SPME 3D FFT optimization (MK-41) across solvated protein systems (4.2k, 6.7k, 23.6k DHFR).

context: Head-to-head OpenMM CUDA vs Prolix Pallas v2.6 benchmark harness (bench_e2e_ensemble_buckets.py, MK-42).
lesson: Four pitfalls broke OpenMM CUDA comparisons and multi-bucket PME grid scaling: (1) spawning b1-openmm/bin/python without adding b1-openmm/lib, site-packages/nvidia/*/lib, and CUDA toolkit lib64 to LD_LIBRARY_PATH caused dlopen(libOpenMMCUDA.so) to fail on missing libcufft.so/libnvrtc.so and fall back to OpenCL; (2) unpacking bond_params as (k_b, r0_b) instead of MolecularBundle's canonical (r0_b, k_b) (and (th0_a, k_a) for angles) corrupted harmonic bond lengths/force constants; (3) wrapping truncated water coordinates atom-by-atom via jnp.mod(pos, box) split boundary waters across opposite periodic faces, causing OpenMM SETTLE to diverge to NaN; (4) multi-bucket EnsemblePlan runs ([8192, 25000]) need bucket-mapped PROLIX_PME_GRID_POINTS ('8192:48,25000:64') and PROLIX_PME_GRID_POINTS included in _SINGLE_INFERENCE_CACHE / _STACKED_INFERENCE_CACHE keys so each bucket compiles with its appropriate PME FFT grid.

context: Pallas v2.7 Blackwell sm_120 register-spill / stack-overflow fix (MK-43), vectorized float32 Langevin BAOAB O-step thermal noise (MK-44), and uniform bundle precision / lax.cond reference_position.dtype normalization (MK-45) across settle.py, batched_simulate.py, ensemble_plan.py, and neighbor_list.py.
lesson: Three critical lessons from multi-GPU benchmarking on NVIDIA L40S (sm_89), NVIDIA H200 (sm_90), and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120): (1) MK-43: While standalone _pallas_nonbonded_nl_batch on Hopper/Ada benefits from num_stages=2 on large grids, passing num_stages=2 ('nonbonded_nl' with grid_blocks >= 256) plus a 59th blk_has_bonded_ref buffer and nested runtime jax.lax.cond around vector force stores inside the 7-branch _megakernel caused Triton on sm_120 to spill tile registers to per-thread local memory (5.5x slowdown at 8k and CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS stack overflow at DHFR mixed B=4). Dedicated kernel_kind='megakernel' in resolve_pallas_compiler_params (and all Pallas kernels on Blackwell cc >= 10.0) must use num_warps=4, num_stages=1 across all grid sizes and keep _run_k_tiles force writebacks branchless at runtime (compile-time if total_bonded_blocks == 0: _pl_store else: _pl_atomic_add_1d with 58 input refs). (2) MK-44: In mixed precision mode (jax_enable_x64=True), _langevin_step_o_constrained in settle.py executed jax.random.split(key, n_w + 1) plus 2*n_w per-water float64 jax.random.normal calls every step (24,577 Threefry calls per replica!). Sampling a single contiguous z6_all = jax.random.normal(split_w, (n_w, 6), dtype=jnp.float32).astype(r_water.dtype) tensor once per step and generating isotropic Gaussian thermal noise in float32 before casting to momentum.dtype eliminates thousands of per-step PRNG splits and float64 Box-Muller evaluations. (3) MK-45: Constructing MolecularBundle from .npz while jax_enable_x64=True can leave positions as float64 and masses as float32, causing float64->float32 scatter incompatibilities in settle.py and reference_position.dtype mismatches in _maybe_rebuild_nl; always normalize bundle floating-point leaves to a uniform dtype and cast p_w.astype(r_o.dtype) in _maybe_rebuild_nl.
action: Use kernel_kind='megakernel' (num_warps=4, num_stages=1; and num_stages=1 for cc >= 10.0) and branchless 58-arg _run_k_tiles writeback in _pallas_bonded_and_nonbonded_nl_fused_batch, sample all Langevin BAOAB thermal noise in vectorized float32 before casting to state dtype, and cast p_w.astype(r_o.dtype) in _maybe_rebuild_nl.

context: Pallas v3.0 optimization campaign (MK-46..MK-49) on NVIDIA L40S (sm_89): fused Pallas BAOAB+SETTLE+RATTLE integrator kernels, per-replica NL rebuild_mask early-exit, spatially pruned 32x32 nonbonded block megakernel, and separable (32, 16) YZ-plane factorized SPME spread/gather.
lesson: Four engineering lessons from Pallas v3.0 on NVIDIA L40S (Job 28062261): (1) MK-46: Fusing the ~18 per-step XLA scatter/gather/elementwise kernels in settle.py into two 2D-grid (B, cdiv(N_atoms, 64) + cdiv(N_waters, 32)) Pallas kernels (pallas_baoab_pre_force and pallas_baoab_post_force) with a precomputed loop-invariant _iwg_precomputed water/ghost mask and in-kernel ghost pinning speeds up BAOAB+SETTLE by 2.26x (0.1199 ms -> 0.0530 ms on 8k bucket). Crucially, in JAX Pallas Triton lowering (_minus), lax.neg_p inspects x.type and raises AttributeError: 'TypedNdArray' object has no attribute 'type' whenever unary '-' is applied to a scalar constant jnp.asarray(c, dtype=dtype); always negate Python floats before jnp.asarray(-c, dtype=dtype) or write zero - expr. (2) MK-47: Threading rebuild_mask: bool[B] and old_idx into _build_cell_stencil_buffers_batched and _pallas_prune_and_encode_cell_list_batch with input_output_aliases={15: 0} lets non-rebuilding replicas exit in O(1) at the top of the Pallas cell-prune CTA while preserving old_idx[b] in-place. (3) MK-48: Gating 32-atom nonbonded row blocks on jnp.max(mask_i_b) > 0 and gating q_j/sig_j/eps_j global loads on jnp.max((r_sq < cutoff_sq).astype(int32)) > 0 with reciprocal-multiply PBC wrapping reduces 8k force evaluation to 0.1313 ms and 25k ragged force evaluation to 0.1366 ms. (4) MK-49: Factorizing the 64-point 4x4x4 SPME B-spline stencil into a precomputed (32, 16) YZ-plane outer product outside the 4-iteration X loop and gating spread atomics on (mask_n > 0) & (abs(q) > 0) boosts L40S end-to-end throughput to 708.54 ns/day on Small (B=2, 53.3% of OpenMM mixed), 609.27 ns/day on Medium (B=2, 49.0% of OpenMM mixed), and 117.17 ns/day on DHFR (98.67 ns/day at B=1).
action: Never apply unary '-' to jnp.asarray(c, dtype=dtype) constants inside Pallas Triton kernels; precompute _iwg_precomputed outside the MD while_loop; pass rebuild_mask and old_idx with input_output_aliases={15: 0} for multi-replica NL rebuilds; and factorize 3D B-spline stencils into (BLOCK_N, 16) YZ-plane outer products.

lesson: Eight engineering lessons from Pallas v3.1 (MK-50..MK-53) verified on NVIDIA L40S (sm_89): (1) MK-50: Precomputing _iwg_precomputed once outside init_fn/apply_fn eliminates the 614.4M-element jnp.isin(all_indices, real_idx_flat) water mask in init_fn (cutting fast_reseed_fn from 3.71 ms to 0.097 ms at B=16, 38.2x speedup); warming _fused_nl_run(rng) on Call 1 and sharing _STACKED_NL_SEED_CACHE[(B, N_pad)] + _STACKED_JIT_FN_CACHE across homogeneous/heterogeneous runs cuts warm B=1 DHFR EnsemblePlan.run from 131.03 ms/step (un-warmed Call 2) to 0.566-0.588 ms/step (293.9-305.3 ns/day, 3.09x over v3.0) and avoids recompiling across mutant batches. (2) MK-51: Slicing first_cols = nbr_b[:, :, ::_NB_BLOCK_K] BEFORE padding in _compute_max_k_tiles avoids a 76.8 MB * B neighbor-list copy on every force step when N % 32 != 0; bounding _nb_nl_kernel/_megakernel K-tile loops by max_k_tiles[b, i_block] and providing spatially sorted 32x32 TilePairNeighborList + pallas_nonbonded_tile_pairs reaches 0.192-0.222 ms/rep on 23,558-atom DHFR. (3) MK-52: Replacing vmap(jnp.argsort) in _build_cell_stencil_buffers_batched on GPU with a 2D-grid (B, cdiv(N, 128)) Pallas atomic cell-binning kernel (_make_pallas_bin_cells_kernel) speeds up cell binning by 1.96x-3.35x (0.054-0.062 ms/rep vs 0.106-0.208 ms/rep). (4) Zero-copy input_output_aliases rule: Wrapping old_idx.reshape(B*N*K) in jnp.pad(..., (0, 1)) and slicing nbr_flat[:-1] around pallas_call(..., input_output_aliases={15: 0}) forces XLA to allocate and copy 76.8 MB/rep (1.23 GB at B=16) on every MD step; gate use_scratch_slot = bool(interpret) so GPU passes old_idx directly with masked stores (mask=in_b & (k_slot < K_cap)), cutting B=16 NL rebuild time from 5.54 ms -> 2.98 ms (1.86x) and pure while_loop step time from 0.858 -> 0.640 ms/step/rep (+34.1%). (5) MK-53: Gating SPME spread/gather CTAs on active_q = is_real & (abs(q) > 0) and supporting 4x4x4 sub-grid spatial sorting via compute_pme_spatial_perm reaches 0.029 ms/rep total 64^3 SPME at B=16 (spread=0.013, fft=0.009, gather=0.007 ms/rep) and 1,291.06 ns/day on Small (97.2% of OpenMM CUDA mixed), 1,206.31 ns/day on Medium (97.0% of OpenMM mixed), and 232.2-305.3 ns/day on heterogeneous DHFR mutant screens (B=1..32). (6) Pallas interpret=True scalar load rule: Always pass a 1D index array (box_base + jnp.zeros((1,), dtype=jnp.int32),) and index [0] to _pl_load. (7) CPU float64 parity rule: Keep PROLIX_USE_PALLAS_SETTLE default empty so CPU defaults to pure-JAX float64 (< 1e-12 A 100-step parity vs settle_langevin). (8) Timed benchmark window rule: Record warm_s = time.perf_counter() - t0_warm immediately after block_until_ready and use np.all(np.isfinite(np.asarray(...))) so XLA does not compile per-variant jnp.isfinite kernels inside the timed window.
action: Never wrap Pallas input_output_aliases buffers in jnp.pad on GPU (gate scratch slots on bool(interpret)); slice before padding in _compute_max_k_tiles; warm _fused_nl_run on Call 1 and share _STACKED_NL_SEED_CACHE + _STACKED_JIT_FN_CACHE; and keep timed windows free of post-run jnp.isfinite dispatches.

lesson: Five engineering lessons from Pallas v3.2 (MK-54..MK-57) verified on NVIDIA L40S (sm_89, Job 28376913): (1) MK-54: Inverting jax.vmap(lax.while_loop) into a single scalar-predicate lax.while_loop over the batched (B, ...) carry (@custom_vmap _any_replica_true) and splitting execution into an outer NL-rebuild while_loop + inner nl_update_every-step fixed-NL while_loop (_two_level_runner) eliminates both _while_batcher's per-step lax.select copy (76.8 MB/rep = 1.23 GB at B=16) and _maybe_rebuild_nl's per-step kConditional copy of neighbor.idx, turning f_non_step_overhead negative (-15.9 ms at B=1 to -47.4 ms at B=16). (2) MK-55: Generating 10-round counter-based Philox-2x32 + Box-Muller Gaussian thermal noise (_philox2x32_box_muller_pair) directly in Triton registers inside _pre_kernel eliminates ~218 MB/step of HBM traffic and 2 XLA RNG kernel launches at B=16, while gating the +1 scratch slot on bool(interpret) and masking offs_a < N inside _pre_kernel/_post_kernel removes per-step jnp.pad when N % 64 != 0 (BAOAB = 0.089 ms/rep at B=1, 0.011 ms/rep at B=16). (3) MK-56: Computing max_k_tiles = (jnp.max(occ_pad, axis=-1) + 31) // 32 once per NL rebuild on NeighborList, hoisting precompute_static_nl_exclusion_tables outside lax.while_loop, masking offs_i < N and offs < B_real/A_real/D_real inside _megakernel without per-step jnp.pad on atom or bonded topology arrays, and routing pure-solvent blocks (nb_pid >= first_pure_water_block) to direct _pl_store instead of _pl_atomic_add_1d cuts MK-48 megakernel time on 23,558-atom DHFR from 0.222 ms to 0.061 ms/rep at B=1 (3.64x speedup) and 0.090 ms/rep at B=16. (4) MK-57: Routing inference MD steps through return_forces=True (and compute_energy=False in pallas_bonded_and_nonbonded_nl_fused) skips e_out_ref stores and scalar energy reductions (jnp.sum(e_blk) and jnp.sum(Q * theta_norm)), while 3D Morton-sorting TilePairNeighborList (with custom_vjp _morton_gather_atom_axis) cuts MK-51 tile-pair evaluation on DHFR by 55.9x (2.899 ms -> 0.052 ms at B=1, 0.011 ms/rep at B=16). (5) End-to-End L40S Results: On 23,558-atom DHFR, Prolix Pallas v3.2 reaches 0.203 ms/step (852.63 ns/day) at B=1 single (1.96x faster than OpenMM CUDA mixed 0.397 ms/step = 435.6 ns/day, 1.09x faster than OpenMM single 782.5 ns/day) and 0.123 ms/step/var (1,404.17 ns/day) at B=32 heterogeneous mutant screen (3.66x faster than v3.1), while mixed precision (float64 SETTLE/coordinates) reaches 503.29 ns/day (0.343 ms/step/rep) at B=4 and 581.17 ns/day (0.297 ms/step/var) at B=32.
action: Use scalar while_loop(vmap) with two-level fixed-NL inner loops for multi-replica MD, generate Langevin thermal noise in registers via Philox-2x32, attach max_k_tiles to NeighborList at rebuild time, use direct _pl_store for pure-water blocks (nb_pid >= first_pure_water_block), and enable return_forces=True / compute_energy=False on inference MD trajectories.

context: Pallas v3.3 6-Axis Realistic Benchmark Panel & Cross-Regime Bottleneck Elimination Campaign (MK-58..MK-61) on NVIDIA L40S (sm_89, Jobs 28520600 & 28532308) and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120, Job 28533797): mixed-precision f64-state/f32-force-position dual writeout + register-fori_loop RATTLE (MK-58), non-cubic (Kx,Ky,Kz) SPME + isotropic barostat G_iso scaling + 2-step RESPA PME impulse (MK-59), native GPU tile-pair builder + skin-triggered outer NL rebuilds (MK-60), and active-atom grid clamping + fused 2-pass pallas_gbsa_dense (MK-61).
lesson: Six engineering lessons from Pallas v3.3 (MK-58..MK-61): (1) MK-58 & Pallas Triton Loop Unrolling: Emitting a pre-cast float32 coordinate buffer (pos_f32_out_ref) alongside float64 state updates in _pallas_baoab_pre_force_batch and accepting float32 forces in _pallas_baoab_pre/post_force_batch eliminates two full-array XLA f64<->f32 casts per step, cutting DHFR mixed B=1 step time on L40S from 0.509 ms to 0.365 ms (474.05 ns/day, beating OpenMM CUDA mixed 0.397 ms/step) and 0.211 ms/step/rep (818.51 ns/day, 1.88x OpenMM) at B=16/32. Crucially, inside Pallas Triton kernels, Python-unrolled `for _ in range(8):` loops over 4-slot 3D vector constraint updates (`_rattle_shake_cluster_vec3` and `_rattle_vel_cluster_vec3`, plus a redundant pre-O-step velocity RATTLE call) inline 136 vector constraint iterations into the LLVM IR of `_do_rattle`, causing a ~7-minute Triton/LLVM register-allocator compile stall per batch size; replacing Python `for` with `jax.lax.fori_loop` (lowered to an `scf.for` loop in Triton IR) and removing the redundant pre-O velocity RATTLE cuts compile time from ~7 min to <30s and speeds up RATTLE BAOAB to 0.1046 ms/rep at B=1 and 0.0341 ms/rep at B=4. (2) MK-59: Supporting 3-tuple (Kx, Ky, Kz) SPME grids (e.g. 96x96x64 on 92,224-atom ApoA1) cuts 3D FFT time by 20.5% and gather by 12.2%, reaching 219.2 ns/day/rep (876.8 ns/day agg at B=4 = 368,896 real atoms), while 2-step RESPA PME (pme_every=2) + skin-triggered NL checks (nl_check_every=10) speed up DHFR E2E MD by 1.35x at B=1 and 1.78x at B=4 (0.1127 ms/step/rep = 1,532.8 ns/day/rep). (3) MK-60: Building 32x32 Morton-sorted tile pairs on GPU via `build_tile_pair_neighbor_list_gpu` speeds up tile-pair NL construction by 148.4x on L40S (46.93 ms vs 6,966.12 ms) and 137.7x on Blackwell (30.61 ms vs 4,214.11 ms), while MK-51 Morton tile-pair custom VJPs accelerate `jax.value_and_grad` wrt (r, q, sigma, epsilon) by 3.94x-5.94x on 8k proteins and 10.58x-11.24x on 25k DHFR. (4) MK-61: Clamping 2D Pallas launch grids to `cdiv(n_active_atoms, BLOCK)` keeps 16.8%-occupancy ragged buckets (4,199 atoms in 25,000 bucket) within 3.6% of 8,192-bucket step time at B=1 (0.3085 vs 0.2977 ms), while `pallas_gbsa_dense` with `nonbonded_cutoff=0.0` for `box=None` implicit solvent bundles reaches 29,326 ns/day on 1UAO (12.27x OpenMM CUDA), 8,541 ns/day on 1VII (3.12x OpenMM), and 7,064 ns/day on 1CRN (2.97x OpenMM) at B=64. (5) OpenMM Subprocess Rule: Never instantiate an OpenMM CUDA Context inside the same Python process as JAX GPU, and never override `.venv`'s `OPENMM_PLUGIN_DIR` with a non-existent external conda path; serialize the OpenMM System to XML and time it in an isolated subprocess with `.venv`'s `nvidia/*/lib` and `/orcd/software/core/001/pkg/cuda/*/lib64` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
action: Always use `jax.lax.fori_loop` instead of Python-unrolled `for` loops for iterative constraint solvers (`_rattle_shake_cluster_vec3` / `_rattle_vel_cluster_vec3`) inside Pallas Triton kernels; set `nonbonded_cutoff=0.0` in `physics_system_from_bundle` when `box_size is None` and `has_implicit_solvent=True`; and run OpenMM CUDA baseline timings in an isolated subprocess without overriding `.venv`'s `OPENMM_PLUGIN_DIR`.
